#23369. Breaking: DiScoFormer: One transformer for density and score, across distributions

📅 29 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (818 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: DiScoFormer: One transformer for density and score, across distributions

📅 29 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many problems in machine learning and the sciences come down to the same task: you have a collection of data points and want to recover the distribution they came from—which values are common, and which are rare.
  • Recent findings suggest that diffusion-based generative models (the technology behind AI image generators like Stable Diffusion and DALL-E) start from random noise and repeatedly follow the score, turning that noise into a realistic image.
  • Extracting the density and score from a finite sample is challenging, and today's tools force a trade-off between generalizability and accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Tech report: arxiv.org/abs/2511.05924.

Many problems in machine learning and the sciences come down to the same task: you have a collection of data points and want to recover the distribution they came from—which values are common, and which are rare. Pinning down that distribution means estimating two quantities: the distribution's density and, more useful as dimensionality grows, its score. The density is the smooth version of a histogram—high where points cluster and low where they're scarce. The score—the gradient of the log-density—points in the direction the density rises fastest: move a point along the score and it heads toward a more probable region.

Recent findings suggest that diffusion-based generative models (the technology behind AI image generators like Stable Diffusion and DALL-E) start from random noise and repeatedly follow the score, turning that noise into a realistic image. The same score drives Bayesian sampling and the particle simulations used to model systems such as plasma.

Extracting the density and score from a finite sample is challenging, and today's tools force a trade-off between generalizability and accuracy. One classical approach, kernel density estimation (KDE), computes the density at any location from the data points around it: the closer and more numerous they are, the higher the density. It needs no training and applies to any distribution, but its accuracy falls off sharply as dimensionality grows. Alternatively, neural score-matching models trained to predict the score stay accurate even in high dimensions, but each needs to learn the distribution and must be retrained from scratch for another.

We introduce a new solution called the DiScoFormer (Density and Score Transformer)—one model that, given a set of data points, estimates both the density and the score of the distribution in a single forward pass without retraining.

Industry observers note that diScoFormer maps an entire sample to the density and score of the distribution behind it using stacked layers of transformer blocks. The model utilizes cross-attention, which allows it to evaluate density and score at any point—not just where you have data. Score and density share a mathematical relationship: score is the gradient of the logarithm of density. We leverage this by having a shared backbone with two output heads, one for the density and one for the score.

This coupling does more than save parameters. The score head has to match the gradient of the log-density head at every query, so any gap between them is a label-free consistency loss. We use this at inference—hold the context fixed, take a few gradient steps on that consistency loss, and DiScoFormer adapts itself to an out-of-distribution input on the spot, no ground-truth density or score required.

It has been revealed that there's a mathematical reason why the transformer architecture fits this task. Kernel density estimation has a single bandwidth—how far each point's influence reaches, fixed in advance and applied identically everywhere. Attention is a strict generalization of it: we analytically show that a single attention head's weights are nearly a Gaussian kernel over the data, so one cross-attention block can already reproduce KDE's density and score. From there the model goes further, learning several such scales at once and adapting them to the data. DiScoFormer doesn't discard the classical method for a black box but instead includes KDE as a special case and improves on it.

In a recent development, what data did we use to train DiScoFormer? We relied on Gaussian Mixture Models for two primary reasons. Firstly, GMMs are universal density approximators—with enough components they match essentially any smooth distribution to arbitrarily small error. Secondly, GMMs have closed-form densities and scores, so we always have an exact target to supervise against. We employ both of these properties by drawing a new GMM for every batch, giving the model virtually unlimited examples of target distributions and supervising each against a given GMM's exact density and score.

Across the board, DiScoFormer beats KDE at both density and score estimation, and the gap widens exactly where KDE struggles. In 100 dimensions, it isn't close—against the best hand-tuned KDE, it cuts score error by about 6.5x and density error by more than 37x, and it keeps improving as you add samples, while KDE runs out of memory. It also travels far outside its training data, staying accurate on mixtures with more modes than it ever saw during training and on non-Gaussian shapes like the Laplace and Student-t. KDE's main advantage remains speed, especially when datasets are small.

The part about DiScoFormer that we find most promising is that score estimation is a shared dependency across many fields, such as generative modeling, Bayesian inference, and scientific computing. A pretrained, plug-in estimator that stays accurate in high dimensions and removes the need to retrain per problem could cut that cost across all of them at once—one model, reused everywhere score and density show up.

We encourage you to read our technical report for more details.

#23368. Tech Report: This year’s bug count just passed 100K

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1034 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: This year’s bug count just passed 100K

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ‘We don’t have a security problem anymore.
  • The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) found and disclosed so far in 2026 surpassed 100,000 on Friday - more than double 2025’s total - and the reason can be summed up in two letters: AI.
  • “It’s kind of wild,” Josh Bressers, VulnCheck’s director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure, told The Register.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘We don’t have a security problem anymore. We have a data problem now’.

Chalk up a new record for vulns. The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) found and disclosed so far in 2026 surpassed 100,000 on Friday - more than double 2025’s total - and the reason can be summed up in two letters: AI.

“It’s kind of wild,” Josh Bressers, VulnCheck’s director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure, told The Register. “The thing that almost scares the bejesus out of me is while 100K sounds like a lot, in a couple years we're going to say, remember when it was only 100K?”.

It has been revealed that as of the time of our interview, about 4 pm UTC on Friday, VulnCheck counted 100,222 CVEs, he stated. Microsoft alone added 1,094 security flaws to the total count on Tuesday, following 1,474 vulnerabilities the month before.

Recent findings suggest that “There's no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we're seeing.” All the major CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) - these are the organizations authorized by the CVE program to assign unique identifiers to security vulnerabilities - like VulnCheck, Microsoft, Oracle, GitHub, and other large enterprise IT vendors “are just screaming into the atmosphere right now,” Bressers noted. “It’s AI.”.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the percentage of these bugs that are exploited in the wild remains relatively consistent. About 1.4 percent (1,363) of the CVEs published this year have been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

“But obviously, as the number of CVEs grows, [1 percent] of 1,000 is a lot different than [1 percent] of 100,000,” Bressers said.

In a recent development, plus, as other security researchers have documented, the window between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits – often by reverse engineering the patch while end users are still applying the fix – is rapidly shrinking. This is also thanks to AI.

In a recent development, from January to June, 88 percent of the exploitation observed by CrowdStrike using public proof-of-concept (PoC) code occurred within 48 hours of the code's release. The security firm mentioned China-linked groups such as Vault Panda and Genesis Panda moved even faster, launching attacks within 24 hours of disclosure.

Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026. This window has closed even further during the second half of the year, which also seems to coincide with the AI-induced vulnpocalypse.

“It’s often just hours,” Bressers noted, noting 14 make-me-root vulnerabilities that VulnCheck disclosed on Friday in Copeland refrigeration controllers. Two are under active exploitation. These are the devices that Iranian hackers abused to spoil food and spark fires in supermarkets across Europe.

“We published those CVEs, and literally minutes later, we were seeing hits on our honey pots,” Bressers said about the Copeland device vulnerabilities. “We’ve hit a point where with anything that looks interesting, someone is taking that information and seeing what they can do with it. Is it AI driven? Probably. It'd be hard to say it's not, because we've seen it really ramp up recently.”.

This influx of software bugs requires a sea change in how the entire industry approaches vulnerability disclosure and patching.

Sources indicate that “We don't have a security problem anymore,” Bressers stated. “We have a data problem now. Instead of obsessing over vulnerabilities, we need to start looking at things like heat maps for infrastructure, and figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you. The CISA BOD helps with that.”.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) in June issued a cybersecurity directive that replaces flat-deadline vulnerability management policies. Instead of prioritizing patching based solely on CVSS severity scores, the directive instructs organizations to prioritize based on specific risk criteria, including whether the asset is internet-exposed, under active exploitation, and whether an attacker can automate the exploit.

“It's telling people to figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you, and then put those at the top of the list, instead of just saying we're going to fix all the criticals,” Bressers noted.

AI-generated vulnerability disclosures also create huge headaches for open source software developers and maintainers, which Bressers describes as a security problem “super close to my heart.”.

It has been revealed that “You've got individual developers that are drowning in vulnerability reports,” he noted. “You have foundations being crushed by AI agents scraping their data or downloading their packages, millions of times a day, and it's straining the seams absolutely everywhere you look. The one thing I can say with certainty is: The way we at the moment do things has to change, and it's going to have to change fairly soon.”.

Different open source projects have taken different approaches to solving this concern. The Eclipse Foundation, which houses the Open VSX Registry, in April rolled out a “managed tier” for enterprise customers and other organizations running Open VSX at scale.

Instead of using the free, open source version, the managed version guarantees a 99.95 percent uptime SLA backed by service credits. Its customers include AWS, IBM, Google, Cursor, and Windsurf. This paid option means commercial customers who rely on the registry help fund its ongoing maintenance - and their own platforms’ security and performance.

Meanwhile, curl’s maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, citing an “avalanche of vulnerability reports," updated its bug reporting rules last month. As of October 26, all low- and medium-severity reports go directly into the public GitHub repository, with only the high- and critical-flaws receiving private handling.

Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty program this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team.

Recent findings suggest that “A lot more needs to happen, and I think it is going to be a challenge to enact some of this change,”  Bressers said. “When a package registry drastically changes something, people start freaking out, and the world is going to end, and people on LinkedIn are complaining - a lot of people are hesitant. No one wants to be the first to jump into the alligator-filled pool. That's one of our challenges.”®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every Eval Ever (EEE) and Hugging Face Community Evals are now intercompatible.
  • Sources indicate that EEE launched in February 2026 as a project of the EvalEval Coalition, the first cross-institutional effort to improve how AI evaluation results get reported by both first and third party evaluators.
  • Recent findings suggest that evaluation results are how we measure model capabilities, compare models against each other, and reason about safety and governance, and yet they are scattered and hard to compare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every Eval Ever (EEE) and Hugging Face Community Evals are now intercompatible. We enable cross-posting and interpreting evaluation results, while linking to open models, leaderboards, and a unified standardized metadata store.

Sources indicate that EEE launched in February 2026 as a project of the EvalEval Coalition, the first cross-institutional effort to improve how AI evaluation results get reported by both first and third party evaluators. Hugging Face launched Community Evals in February 2026 to decentralize how benchmark scores get reported on the Hub. Combined, they patch gaps in how people, researchers, and policymakers trust, understand, and choose evaluations and models.

Recent findings suggest that evaluation results are how we measure model capabilities, compare models against each other, and reason about safety and governance, and yet they are scattered and hard to compare. They live in papers, leaderboards, blog posts, and harness logs, among others, each in its own format. The same model on the same benchmark often returns different scores depending on who ran it and how; LLaMA 65B, for one, has been reported at both 63.7 and 48.8 on MMLU. These gaps can arise from evaluation settings that we found are commonly unreported.

In a recent development, EEE is our fix for the reporting side. It's one JSON schema for an evaluation result that records:.

Recent findings suggest that the schema was built with feedback from researchers and policy researchers, and it takes in results from any source, so harness logs, leaderboard scrapes, and paper numbers all end up in the same shape. The GitHub repository has the converters, examples, and a contributor guide. Since launching, the datastore on Hugging Face has grown to around 229,000 evaluation results across more than 22,000 models and 2,200 benchmarks, pulled from 31 different reporting formats. Reproducing just those runs from scratch would cost somewhere in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, which is a reasonable argument for not letting the data scatter once someone has paid to generate it.

Learn more about the schema and how to contribute here.

It has been revealed that now, it comes with better integration and attribution. Contributors can now send EEE results to Hugging Face Community Evals. We built a converter that takes your EEE records and writes the small YAML files Hugging Face expects, so you don't have to keep the same result in two formats by hand.

This is latest functionality for everyone who reports or reads evaluations, not only existing EEE contributors. First-party evaluators reporting on their own models and third-party evaluators reporting on someone else's can both submit to Community Evals and to EEE, and anyone browsing the Hub gets results that trace back to a full record. When you submit your data through your organization's official Hugging Face account, your results show up with a verified checkmark on EvalEval, a signal to readers that the numbers come straight from the source. The rest of this post walks through what Community Evals are and what the converter does.

Hugging Face Community Evals has two sides.

In a recent development, A benchmark lives in a dataset repo that registers itself by adding an eval.yaml. Once registered, that dataset page collects and displays a leaderboard of every score reported against it across the Hub. The list of official benchmarks grows over time.

A model's scores live in .eval_results/*.yaml inside the model repo. They show up on the model card and feed into the matching benchmark leaderboard. Both the model author's own results and results submitted by anyone else through a pull request get aggregated, and each score carries a badge saying whether it was author-submitted, community-submitted, or independently verified. Anyone can add a score to any model by opening a PR with the right YAML file, and the model author can close PRs or hide results on their own repo.

Here is what one of these leaderboards looks like:.

Community Evals Leaderboard for Humanity's Last Exam on the Hub.

This is where EEE and Community Evals fit together. When you send a result to both, two things happen: First, your score appears on the Hugging Face model page and gets pulled into the benchmark's leaderboard. And second, it carries a source badge that links straight back to the full EEE record, where the generation config, the harness version, the reproducibility notes, and any instance-level data live.

An Evaluation (MMLU-Pro) from EEE Datastore (a) cross-linked at the file level to a Hugging Face model card (b). The Source EvalEval badge links to the full JSON record.

The two destinations do different jobs toward the same goal. Hugging Face puts your result where people look at models, with a link back to the source. EEE keeps the full structured record that makes the result interpretable, and powers Eval Cards on top of it. Send your data to both and the same evaluation ends up visible and legible at once, which is the point of reporting one at all.

You can see that cross-compatibility below. The same GPQA scores that surface on the model card above also render in Eval Cards, which composes the EEE run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record. Same evaluation, a different surface:.

It has been revealed that hugging Face stores eval scores in the model repo as a YAML under .eval_results/. The required fields are just the benchmark dataset, the task, and the value. The source block is the part that creates the backlink to EEE.

The converter fills this in from your existing records. It maps source_data.hf_repo to dataset.id, evaluation_name to task_id, score_details.score to value, and evaluation_timestamp to date, then drops in the datastore object URL as the source link to the per-record EEE JSON. It presently handles four of the official benchmarks: MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HLE, and GSM8K.

The converter does more than reshape fields. You point it at one EEE datastore collection and it downloads that collection along with the records it references, checks the object hashes, and finds the scores that map to a supported benchmark. Before it writes anything live it audits what already exists: it reads every .eval_results YAML on the model's main branch and in open PRs, and compares by dataset and task rather than by filename. If a score is already there it is marked already_present, if a different score is there it is flagged as a score_conflict, and if the model repo doesn't resolve on the Hub it is marked missing_hf_model. Everything else is marked ready.

In a recent development, nothing gets pushed without your sign-off. The tool writes local YAML previews and a review file you can inspect, reveals a report of what is ready and what needs attention, and only opens PRs after you type OPEN PRS and enter a commit message. Reruns reuse the cached results for a collection unless you pass --force.

Sources indicate that the converter's review step. Excluded entries (here, models with no matching Hub repo) are listed with their EEE source URLs, and the ready PRs wait on an explicit OPEN PRS confirmation.

Submit your full records to the EEE datastore.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forensic report finds Blackwell's fingerprint in DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group models.

US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer.

Will DePue, who left the AI giant earlier this year to launch Unemployment Labs, an AI research consultancy, published forensic evidence showing that "DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models.".

Sources indicate that "This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it," stated DePue in a social media post. "When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern – a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.".

Industry observers note that it doesn't sound that insane. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang followed from revelations that he had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who, in 2023, founded Singapore-based Megaspeed International. That company is reportedly under investigation by US authorities for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

Huang's departure coincides with a renewed push to tighten US chip export controls. House Speaker Mike Johnson supports the idea. And there are at least four bills awaiting consideration that aim to limit China's access to leading edge AI tech: the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, Match Act, and the Cloud Security Act.

On Monday, US Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) cited Jensen Huang's "relationship with a suspected Chinese spy" as a justification for passing the AI Overwatch Act, which would codify the Trump administration's existing chip export controls. The Trump administration on Thursday remarked it's not sure whether Alice Huang was a spy, an allegation denied by Beijing and presently under investigation by the FBI.

In a recent development, whatever the case, the current rules clearly are not working. Only a few weeks ago, Lava, an Israel-based security company, said it had found "32 Nvidia B300 GPUs, part of Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra generation, through publicly exposed monitoring endpoints with IP addresses geolocated to China.".

These GPUs, Lava noted, are subject to US export controls [PDF]. The security biz mentioned its findings followed from the exposure of monitoring systems intended for internal infrastructure management that were publicly exposed.

The analysis published through DePue's consultancy, "Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs," takes a different approach: analyzing the published weights of various models from Chinese AI labs.

As described in the report, model weights – the parameters that change in relation to training data – must be initialized with some value. One method for doing so involves a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox. The algorithm starts with a seed value that produces the same set of initial values whenever it's run.

Using PyTorch, initialization can be done by creating multiple GPU threads that work in parallel, with the help of Nvidia's cuRAND library. And because this process is not truly random, it's possible to select a chip and a seed value, generate the initial weights for that hardware and compare that pattern to a model's published weights.

It has been revealed that "I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models," mentioned DePue. "In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models – including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3 – were initialized on Nvidia Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in Nvidia's flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.".

Noting that this is the first time MiniMax and Ant Group have been publicly linked to usage of Nvidia's Blackwell, he also cited several limitations to his approach. One is that usage of Blackwell GPUs doesn't prove where the GPUs were located, so it's possible some of these Chinese labs used this hardware through US providers – a loophole the Cloud Security Act aims to close.

In a recent development, dePue's report includes initial seed values that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Nvidia's Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, for those who wish to attempt to reproduce the results. DuPue claims that multiple senior researchers, both independent and inside frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, have confirmed the result.

Coincidentally, OpenAI and Anthropic have each complained about Chinese labs copying their models through distillation, a pastime also noted by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. ®.

Why Specialization Is Inevitable

📅 30 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that those who follow Dharma AI already know that we view specialization as one of the defining principles of effective AI systems, shaping everything from cost and performance to reliability and sovereignty.
  • In this article, we explore and interpret ideas from AI Must Embrace Specialization via Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence (Goldfeder, Wyder, LeCun, & Shwartz-Ziv, 2026).
  • Industry observers note that the conventional expectation is reasonable: as AI systems grow more capable, they should also grow more general.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that those who follow Dharma AI already know that we view specialization as one of the defining principles of effective AI systems, shaping everything from cost and performance to reliability and sovereignty. Few papers have articulated that case as rigorously as the 2026 work by Goldfeder, Wyder, LeCun, and Shwartz-Ziv.

In this article, we explore and interpret ideas from AI Must Embrace Specialization via Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence (Goldfeder, Wyder, LeCun, & Shwartz-Ziv, 2026). The paper's convergence case — spanning optimization theory, biology, organizational economics, and machine learning — provides both the evidential structure and the intellectual foundation for the discussion that follows. The framing, organization, and editorial synthesis presented here are Dharma's.

Industry observers note that the conventional expectation is reasonable: as AI systems grow more capable, they should also grow more general. Greater capability and broader applicability seem like natural companions — more resources, better methods, and expanded training should produce systems that approach more tasks with increasing confidence.

Sources indicate that the pattern that actually appears is different. The systems that achieve the most significant results in any given domain tend to be the ones most narrowly focused on it. The breakthrough in protein structure prediction came from a system engineered for a single scientific task. The historical milestones of AI, examined closely, reflect intense domain targeting rather than expanding generality.

This pattern recurs. It recurs across domains, across decades, across architectural choices that have almost nothing in common. A pattern this consistent suggests a common cause — one that does not originate inside AI research at all.

In 1997, Wolpert and Macready proved something that rarely surfaces in discussions of AI architecture: no single, general-purpose optimization algorithm outperforms all others across all possible problems (Wolpert & Macready, 1997). The proof is mathematical, not philosophical. Averaged across every conceivable problem a learner might face, every algorithm performs equally well — and equally poorly. An algorithm that gains on one distribution of problems necessarily concedes on others. The performance is redistributed, not multiplied.

Recent findings suggest that the practical implication is direct: “an algorithm wins by being a good fit for the target problem” (Goldfeder et al., 2026). The theorem does not say generality is impossible — it says generality is not a performance advantage. The consistent structural path to outperformance is concentration: trading breadth for fit.

In a recent development, this becomes sharper when finite resources enter the picture. Any real system operates under constraints — finite compute, finite data, finite development time. Given finite energy, an approach that directs available resources toward learning a finite set of tasks will outperform one that distributes those same resources across an unlimited range. The arithmetic is unforgiving: as the task set expands without bound, the resources available per task shrink toward zero. Universal coverage and meaningful performance are, under finite resources, in direct tension.

The conclusion the theorem points toward is not that generality is bad. It is narrower and more operational than that: as the paper states, "universal generality is a theoretical concept, but in practical terms it is a myth" (Goldfeder et al., 2026). What survives contact with real constraints is not the system that tries to do everything — it is the system that fits its target.

The mathematics establishes this as a prediction, not a preference. Whether that prediction holds in the world beyond optimization theory is a different question.

Two other domains arrived at the same prediction before optimization theory gave it a name.

As the paper describes the biological case: every performance gain in one niche comes at a cost elsewhere. A generalist carries traits suited to many environments but optimal for none — competence spread too thin to dominate any particular condition. There are no performance gains without trade-offs; the resources invested in one capability are unavailable for another. Selection favors designs matched to local conditions over those optimized for uniform coverage across all possible environments. The organisms that survive to reproduce are not the most generally capable — they are the most specifically matched. The result, accumulated over evolutionary timescales, is not generalists dominating — it is specialists filling niches. As the paper states: "Specialization is not an accident of biology; it is a predictable consequence of limited resources, competing objectives, and environments that reward performance on a small subset of evolutionarily relevant challenges" (Goldfeder et al., 2026).

According to recent reports, competitive markets follow the same dynamic through different means. Organizations and strategies that fail to meet performance thresholds are eliminated — not through extinction, but through exit, defunding, and replacement by better-matched alternatives. Competition acts as a selection mechanism: it amplifies effective strategies and eliminates ineffective ones. The mechanism has nothing in common with biological selection — no inheritance, no mutation, no evolutionary timescale. The unit of selection is not the organism but the organization, the product, the strategy. Yet the structural pressure is the same: finite resources, performance requirements, and the systematic removal of entities too broadly distributed to excel where it counts. Concentrated capacity outcompetes distributed capacity when performance standards are clear and consistent.

Evolution and markets operate through entirely different mechanisms — different timescales, different units of selection, different inheritance mechanisms. Yet both produce the same outcome under resource pressure: fit over breadth. The theorem predicts this. Biology and markets arrive at it independently. When a third domain arrives at the same finding through different means entirely, the pattern ceases to look like a theorem and begins to look like something more general about how constrained systems behave.

The same pattern has emerged inside machine learning — not derived from optimization theory, but arrived at through the accumulated experience of building systems and watching what improves them.

The clearest form is negative transfer: a measurable degradation that occurs when a system trained on multiple tasks suffers because those tasks compete rather than cooperate (Ruder, 2017). When tasks share structure, training together helps. But when tasks compete for representational capacity, or impose conflicting gradients during training, performance on individual tasks falls below what a dedicated system would achieve. The gain from breadth becomes a cost to depth. It is a documented consequence of dividing finite capacity across tasks that pull against each other. The specialist, facing no such competition, does not pay this cost.

It has been revealed that the architecture of frontier models offers a different form of evidence. Mixture-of-experts systems achieve their breadth not through uniform generality across all parameters, but by routing each input to a specialized subset of the network — activating different experts for different tasks. The paper's authors read this as a structural concession: a system designed to be general achieving its results by recovering specialization internally. This is an argued interpretation, not a demonstrated theorem — these architectures were designed for computational efficiency, and what they imply about generality's limits is a reasonable inference rather than a stated intent. But it is a notable one: the most capable general-purpose systems reach their performance by doing internally what specialist systems do by design.

It has been revealed that the clearest historical example follows the same logic. AlphaFold achieved a step change in protein structure prediction by targeting that specific task with task-specific architecture and training choices (Jumper et al., 2021). Its gains came from narrower focus, not broader coverage. The paper uses AlphaFold as an archetypal case — not as evidence that all specialized systems achieve equivalent gains, but as an unusually clear illustration of the mechanism. That mechanism has appeared repeatedly: the history of AI milestones, the paper notes, frequently reflects intense domain targeting rather than broad competence, even when the results look like demonstrations of general intelligence.

Industry observers note that three distinct places. Three different mechanisms. The same finding.

The picture would be incomplete without addressing one of AI research's most cited observations. Sutton's Bitter Lesson holds that methods relying on domain knowledge are consistently outperformed by methods that scale computation (Sutton, 2019). On its face, this appears to complicate the case for specialization: if scale and generality win, perhaps specialization is only a useful heuristic under resource constraints that will ease as compute becomes cheaper.

Sources indicate that the objection rests on a conflation between two distinct concepts. Domain knowledge refers to hand-coded features, engineered priors, and rules designed to give a system insight into a particular area. The Bitter Lesson targets this — and it is correct to do so. Systems that encode explicit domain knowledge have been consistently outperformed as scale increases.

According to recent reports, domain specialization is different: the decision to direct a system's resources, architecture, and training toward a bounded set of tasks rather than distributing them broadly. This is not the encoding of knowledge about a domain. It is a decision about scope.

The paper draws the distinction precisely:.

"The diminishing usefulness of domain knowledge is distinct from the usefulness of domain specialization. As scaling progresses, we will need to know less about proteins to build a system that does protein folding; however, such a system still benefits from focusing specifically on proteins." (Goldfeder et al., 2026).

Scaling changes what systems can learn from data. It does not change whether concentrating resources on a finite task set outperforms distributing them across an unlimited range. The Bitter Lesson and the specialization argument operate on different dimensions — one describes how knowledge should be acquired, the other describes what a system should be pointed at. Both can be true simultaneously. Scaling changes the mechanisms by which systems learn; it does not dissolve the constraint that makes fit more valuable than breadth.

It has been revealed that across four analytical traditions, the same pattern emerged through different paths. This is not a coincidence that demands explanation. It is the evidence.

When finite resources meet selection pressure — in an optimization problem, an ecosystem, a market, or a training run — fit consistently beats breadth. The specific mechanisms differ. The timescales differ. The units of selection differ. But the structural dynamic is the same, and it produces the same result.

Sources indicate that the theorem does not cause this pattern in biology. Biology does not cause it in markets. Neither causes it in machine learning. They all face the same underlying constraint: performance under scarcity requires concentration. What the theorem establishes mathematically, evolutionary history confirms empirically, competitive markets demonstrate institutionally, and machine learning rediscovers architecturally.

It has been revealed that specialization is not a preference. It is what emerges when finite resources meet the requirement to perform.

Sources indicate that if you're evaluating how domain focus affects AI performance in your organization — or building the case internally for a specialization strategy — we'd like to hear about your context. Get in touch with Dharma AI.

Specialization Beats Scale: A Strategic Variable Most AI Procurement Decisions Overlook — The empirical and strategic complement to this article. Where the No Free Lunch theorem establishes why specialization is structurally predicted, this piece examines the evidence that it outperforms in practice — and why it remains underweighted in most AI procurement decisions.

Text Degeneration: A Production Failure Mode That Most Benchmarks Do Not Track — A documented failure mode that emerges when language models operate outside the boundaries of their effective domain.

Direct Preference Optimization Beyond Chatbots — How preference optimization techniques extend into specialized domains beyond conversational AI — a concrete instantiation of the domain focus strategy this article argues is structurally predicted.

It has been revealed that I would add that in the era of AI Agents, deploying a upcoming hyperspecialized agent with a very narrow domain and less prompts/context, would lead to less hallucinations and less token comsuption. It's cheap and convenient, so is the most probable path in my opinion.

The top line thesis — specialization beats generality — is (forgive me) something of a PGIO (penetrating glimpse into the obvious). I do appreciate the distinction between domain knowledge and domain specialization. They're not the same axis, and conflating them is a common mistake. Regretably, the authors stop right where things get interesting. Domain knowledge's value-add is described as diminishing as scale increases, with no stated floor. Specialization's value-add is described as persisting; not growing, just not eroding the way knowledge does. That's a decline running against a flat line, not two things moving in the same direction at different speeds. The authors never say where that decline runs out, or when investing further in expert content stops paying off — compared to just narrowing scope. A distinction this precise about what specialization is deserves precision about when to stop chasing knowledge and start chasing focus. How much is enough? 10K hours worth (a la Malcolm Gladwell)?

Great point, and I agree that this is where the discussion becomes most interesting.

Industry observers note that it is not possible to say where the decline bottoms out, since neural networks learn representations through superposition rather than assigning individual neurons or subnetworks to specific domains. In other words, it is not possible to isolate parts of the network and claim that they are responsible for domain X or domain Y, as these domains are encoded through overlapping representations. What we can affirm is that it depends on the relationship between breadth of domains in the knowledge base and the number of parameters of the model (the greater the parameters, the greater the capacity to retain knowledge). To answer this question, we would need some way of measuring the amount of domain knowledge contained in the training data, as well as the degree of overlap between those domains in the latent space learned by a highly non-linear neural network. I believe this question is at the moment intractable.

Recent findings suggest that regarding the point at which investing in specialized content ceases to pay off, I believe that this only happens when the objective is to build a genuinely more general-purpose model. If the goal is to use the available resources (parameters) to provide shallow responses across a broad range of topics, then it makes more sense to train on a dataset with broad coverage but relatively little depth in each domain. On the other hand, if the objective is to build a model that solves a finite and relatively small set of tasks, more specialized data will always be the better choice. Naturally, as you increase the size of that task set, you eventually return to the first scenario of wanting a general-purpose model.

The same reasoning applies to the question of when we should pursue greater focus: whenever the scope of the application is itself focused. It is fundamentally a design choice. If you are training a model for open-ended tasks that may receive any type of input, it is better to have a model that responds superficially across many topics than one that responds deeply to only a few. Conversely, if the application has a well-defined scope, it will always be better to train a model specialized for that scope, making more efficient use of its resources instead of spending them on knowledge that will never be required.

That stated, these are very relevant questions, and we hope to address at least part of them through mechanistic interpretability, which is one of the research areas within our R&D efforts. The techniques in this field allow us to observe internal circuits within models, sparsely used neurons, neurons that activate under specific conditions, and other internal mechanisms. This may help us better understand how models work internally and answer some of your questions more directly.

Here’s the whole app: a tiny HTTP server with a health check, and a Dockerfile on Node.js 24, a supported LTS line.

Then build it, run it and check it:.

Recent findings suggest that the build took 8.3 seconds, including pulling node:24-alpine, and the health check answered straight away. The --restart unless-stopped flag brings the container back after a crash or reboot, which I tested later.

That’s a working app, but on plain HTTP, on a high port, with no TLS. Getting it production-ready is the DevOps part I handed to the AI.

An AI-managed VPS isn’t the same as a traditional managed VPS. You still get a self-managed server with full root access, but Hostinger Agent does the work you’d normally do yourself. Agent (previously called Kodee) is an MCP-powered assistant that lives in the dashboard and beside the AI web terminal, and it’s included at no extra cost. You can also connect Claude or Cursor to your server through Hostinger’s MCP server.

I gave it three tasks in plain English.

My prompt: “Check that Docker is installed, then set up a reverse proxy with a free SSL certificate so my demo-app container (port 3000) is served at https://srvXXXXXXX.hstgr.cloud.”.

According to recent reports, it started by looking around: the Docker and Compose versions, which ports were in use, whether a web server was already running, and the OS release. Then it installed Caddy from Caddy’s official repository, configured the proxy and made sure ufw allowed web traffic.

Industry observers note that it read Caddy’s logs to confirm the Let’s Encrypt certificate, which arrived in about 6 seconds. Finally it tested its own work: HTTPS returned 200, and plain HTTP returned a 308 redirect. The whole task took about two minutes.

To give it a real fault, I ran docker stop demo-app and reloaded the site. Then I asked why it was returning a 502 and to fix it.

In a single command, it checked the container state (Exited (137)) and searched Caddy’s logs, where it found connect: connection refused on port 3000. It restarted the container, confirmed /health and HTTPS were back, and even pointed to my docker stop in the terminal history. It also explained that --restart unless-stopped covers crashes and reboots, but not a manual stop.

It has been revealed that A tip it didn’t mention: exit code 137 means Docker had to force-kill the container, because Node running as PID 1 ignores SIGTERM. Add --init to docker run for clean, instant shutdowns.

Industry observers note that this was the most impressive answer. ufw already allowed only those three ports, but Agent noticed port 3000 was still reachable from the internet, because Docker-published ports bypass ufw rules.

Sources indicate that it recreated the container bound to 127.0.0.1:3000, so the app is only reachable through Caddy, and confirmed with an external port check. It left DNS, time sync and Caddy’s local admin port running, explaining that stopping them would break DNS and time sync.

According to recent reports, then I asked it to reboot the server. First it checked that Docker and Caddy start on boot and that the container’s restart policy was set, then it rebooted. The site came back over HTTPS without any help from me.

Nothing I asked for was destructive, so Agent just got on with it: the firewall change, the container rebuild and the reboot all ran without a confirmation prompt.

Industry observers note that the Agent panel says so upfront, noting that terminal commands can run without one. For destructive actions such as reinstalling the OS or restoring a backup, Hostinger’s FAQ says Agent always asks for confirmation first.

Recent findings suggest that one thing worth knowing: to close port 3000, Agent removed and recreated my container. That was harmless for a stateless demo, but a container that keeps data without a volume would lose it. Take a snapshot before massive jobs, and keep the panel in view.

The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded.

In a recent development, in a press conference Saturday, Transportation Secretary Duffy attributed the FAA ground stop to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade. Duffy stated it has yet to be determined whether the matter was incompetence or a faulty router.

In a statement provided to The Register on Saturday, a spokesperson for L3Harris mentioned, “L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”.

The stop was issued on Friday around the middle of the day ET.

Sources indicate that "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," remarked US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement on Friday. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.".

Industry observers note that A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone at the time stated he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement.

The FAA ATCSCC advisory halted departing flights and remarked international flights would be dealt with individually.

The notice noted, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis.".

According to recent reports, doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, stated, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now.".

An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage.".

It has been revealed that the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. ®.

Updated at 0039 UTC Sunday UTC with the administration's explanation for the stop.

Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop.

It has been revealed that CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.”.

Industry observers note that air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its newly introduced Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the firm noted.

ScarfBench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Enterprise Java Framework Migration

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, modernizing enterprise applications is one of the largest and most expensive software engineering activities organizations undertake.
  • Sources indicate that recent advances in coding agents have sparked excitement around AI-assisted modernization.
  • Can AI agents reliably modernize real-world enterprise applications?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

⭐ Star ScarfBench on GitHub.

According to recent reports, modernizing enterprise applications is one of the largest and most expensive software engineering activities organizations undertake. Teams migrate applications across frameworks to improve maintainability, cloud readiness, developer productivity, and access to modern capabilities.

Sources indicate that recent advances in coding agents have sparked excitement around AI-assisted modernization. But an important question remains:.

Can AI agents reliably modernize real-world enterprise applications?

Sources indicate that existing software engineering benchmarks have demonstrated impressive progress in bug fixing and code generation, but framework migration presents a fundamentally different challenge. Success requires not only translating code, but also preserving behavior, adapting build systems, and navigating runtime dependencies.

To address this gap, we introduce ScarfBench (Self-Contained Application Refactoring Benchmark), an open benchmark for evaluating AI agents on cross-framework migration tasks in Enterprise Java.

ScarfBench focuses on migrations across three major Java ecosystems:.

Unlike traditional benchmarks that compare generated code against reference implementations, ScarfBench evaluates whether migrated applications actually build, deploy, and preserve behavior.

Framework migration is much more than replacing annotations.

According to recent reports, A simple repository migration can require changes across dependency injection, persistence configuration, queries, and framework descriptors. Small mistakes in any of these pieces can prevent successful deployment.

Figure: Spring → Jakarta Migration Example.

Framework migration requires translating framework semantics, not just source code.

ScarfBench provides a systematic way to evaluate AI agents on enterprise Java framework migration tasks.

This provides a much more realistic measure of modernization quality.

ScarfBench includes both focused migration tasks and whole-application migrations.

Figure: ScarfBench Construction Pipeline.

Starting from a JSR-based enterprise Java taxonomy, expert migrations create verified implementations across Spring, Jakarta EE, and Quarkus.

We evaluated several state-of-the-art coding agents on ScarfBench.

Despite strong performance on traditional software engineering benchmarks, framework migration remains difficult. Success rates vary considerably across framework pairs and whole-application migrations remain particularly challenging.

Figure: Compile → Deploy → Test Progression.

Compile success consistently exceeds deploy success, which in turn exceeds behavioral success. Build success alone significantly overestimates migration quality.

Figure: Migration Outcomes by Target Framework.

Migration difficulty depends strongly on the target framework, with Jakarta EE proving particularly challenging.

Beyond measuring success rates, ScarfBench helps us understand how agents behave during modernization.

A migrated application is only useful if it actually builds and runs.

We therefore compared agent-reported outcomes against independent build verification.

Claude Code reported successful builds for 29 out of 30 whole applications.

Only 22 of those applications actually built successfully.

Meanwhile, the single application classified as failed by the agent ultimately built correctly.

This suggests that agent self-assessment should not be treated as a reliable signal of migration completion.

Independent build and test validation remains essential.

Framework migrations rarely affect a single file or layer.

Changes in configuration, services, databases, and web components often cascade across the application.

The most frequently visited layers were:.

This suggests that migration is an iterative dependency-resolution process rather than a simple source-to-source transformation.

We used layer revisit frequency as a proxy for migration effort. Layers that required repeated visits typically involved debugging, dependency resolution, or framework adaptation.

Rather than proceeding linearly, agents repeatedly returned to configuration-related artifacts while resolving framework differences and dependency issues.

Not every migration problem originates from source code.

Agents frequently struggled with environmental issues, including:.

These operational concerns often delayed validation even when the source-code migration itself was largely complete.

Figure: Failure Mode Distribution.

Modernization failures span build systems, deployment environments, dependency injection, databases, endpoints, assertions, and infrastructure.

The biggest challenge in framework modernization is not translating Java code.

It is managing the web of dependencies across configuration, infrastructure, and runtime environments.

While frontier agents can automate substantial portions of the migration process, reliable validation and architectural reasoning remain critical for achieving successful outcomes.

ScarfBench helps expose these challenges and provides a standardized way to measure progress toward truly autonomous application modernization.

ScarfBench is designed as an open resource for researchers and practitioners.

It has been revealed that researchers can compare agent architectures and techniques. Practitioners can use ScarfBench to evaluate modernization solutions before deploying them in production environments.

https://github.com/scarfbench/scarfbench.

https://scarfbench.info/leaderboard.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06754.

Framework migration remains one of the largest unsolved problems in AI-assisted software engineering. We hope ScarfBench helps the community measure progress and accelerate the next generation of AI-assisted application modernization.

We invite researchers, practitioners, and framework communities to evaluate their agents, contribute new migration scenarios and help advance the state of the art.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Accessing banned content is as easy as whipping out a thesaurus, Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee hears.
  • Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say.
  • A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Accessing banned content is as easy as whipping out a thesaurus, Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee hears.

Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say.

A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters.

Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms.

"Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said.

It has been revealed that "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable.

"So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently.".

McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not.

"If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added.

"And we know your algorithm would.".

Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same challenges can be observed on Bing, too.

Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an key role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal.

She mentioned that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly.

There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs.

Recent findings suggest that "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content.".

Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories.

With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process.

As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially.

It has been revealed that citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent.

Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures.

Recent findings suggest that the charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more promptly.

Walker stated there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limbo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests.

Sources indicate that meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report, it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny.

Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment.

The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the fresh duties came into force.

England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves.

Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms.

Industry observers note that she said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.'.

"In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered.

"So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for voice AI, latency is a critical parameter. Developers have made tremendous progress in model quality, but the user experience is still often limited by response times. Hugging Face and Cerebras are changing that experience. Today, we demonstrate what becomes possible when an open, modular voice AI architecture is paired with industry-leading inference speed.

Industry observers note that the result is a speech-to-speech experience that feels dramatically more natural. Instead of waiting for an AI to respond, conversations flow with the responsiveness owners expect from human interaction.

It has been revealed that the demo is built as a real-time speech-to-speech pipeline. Each part of the system is modular, open, and replaceable, making it easy for developers to adapt the stack for different assistants, robots, products, or research projects.

This creates a fully open speech-to-speech loop:.

The architecture brings together the strength of the open-source AI ecosystem: Cerebras for fast inference, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4 31B for the language model, and Qwen for text-to-speech. Every layer can be inspected, modified, and extended by the developers.

It has been revealed that today, some production systems see a reasonable median latency while still experiencing frustrating multi-second delays at the P95. Those delays become even more noticeable when tool calls or multimodal steps require multiple turns.

Cerebras helps solve one of the most notable bottlenecks in the stack: the language-model response time. By making inference dramatically faster and more stable, Cerebras allows the rest of the Hugging Face pipeline to shine.

Recent findings suggest that that stability is especially vital at the long tail. Many systems can deliver acceptable median response times, but occasional slow responses still make conversations feel unreliable.

Sources indicate that this same Hugging Face speech-to-speech pipeline already powers Reachy Mini robots, with more than 9,000 robots in the wild. For robots, voice assistants, and embodied AI, responsiveness is not a cosmetic improvement. It is what makes the interaction feel alive.

It has been revealed that the motivation to use Cerebras is therefore not simply cost reduction. It is low latency, predictable performance, and the ability to create real-time experiences that feel natural at scale.

This collaboration reflects a shared belief that the future of AI will be both open and performant. Open-source models, open infrastructure, and breakthrough inference speed together create a foundation for the next generation of conversational AI.

We invite developers to explore the demo, experiment with the code, and help shape what comes next for real-time voice AI.

Repository: huggingface/speech-to-speech.

We even crossed 10k Reachy Minis in the wild 😄.

Fast responses make conversations feel much more comfortable and engaging, and that's exactly what users have been hoping for. 😊 When the delay is reduced, interactions become smoother and more natural, making voice experiences feel less like talking to software and more like having a real conversation.

That gives developers more flexibility to build solutions that fit different needs instead of being locked into a single ecosystem. The combination of strong model quality with impressive inference speed could help unlock many practical applications across education, customer support, accessibility, and beyond. 🚀.

Even the smartest system can feel frustrating if every response takes too long. 📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models.
  • In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.
  • Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.

In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.

Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU: All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP), combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.

This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4(doc).

It has been revealed that context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.

Attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).

Industry observers note that all-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Collabora and Nextcloud pitch alternatives as education customers weigh the cost of losing free services.
  • The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces.
  • According to recent reports, the main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Collabora and Nextcloud pitch alternatives as education customers weigh the cost of losing free services.

The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces.

According to recent reports, the main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the fresh plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news.

Sources indicate that as well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like. Or, for that matter, other US tech giants.

Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the upcoming A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners.

It has been revealed that the new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks.

A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill.

Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud.".

In a recent development, A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't.".

In a recent development, the risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to blueprint, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly.".

Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure. Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted.

Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty.

In a recent development, dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register: "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure.

"Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy.".

Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®.
