AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing Real World VoiceEQ: Measuring the human quality of voice AI

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.
  • Voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface.
  • Over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.

Voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface. From customer support and healthcare to education, entertainment, and personal assistants, speech is increasingly replacing text as the way people interact with AI.

Over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically. Word error rates continue to fall, latency has reached conversational speeds, and many established benchmarks are approaching saturation. Yet anyone who regularly uses voice AI knows something still feels off.

Sources indicate that voice models can sound like different people over the course of a conversation, miss hesitation or uncertainty, and struggle with accents, noise, or emotional speech. Those shortcomings are easy to miss in benchmarks focused on latency and word error rate. People care whether a voice system can truly listen, respond appropriately, and remain natural and reliable in real conversations.

To measure those qualities, we built Real World VoiceEQ—a benchmark designed to evaluate the human quality of voice interaction. It assesses whether voice systems can recognize, produce, and respond to the acoustic information transcripts leave out, from tone and emotion to speaker identity and background context.

Real World VoiceEQ evaluates more than 40 leading proprietary and open-source voice models across 15+ key evaluation dimensions and more than 60 metrics spanning Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), Speech-to-Speech (S2S), and Speech Understanding.

Real World VoiceEQ was developed from more than 1 million individual human ratings collected across different demographics, speaking styles, and acoustic environments. The current benchmark includes 785,000 TTS ratings and 48,000 STS ratings, making it one of the largest human evaluations of voice AI conducted to date.

Every evaluation was conducted using Kairos, our flexible, voice-native evaluation platform. The same infrastructure enables frontier AI labs and enterprises to run custom evaluations tailored to specific use cases, identify granular failure modes in production voice systems, generate human preference data, and continuously improve models through reinforcement learning and human feedback.

The race for a single "best" voice model is giving way to a collection of specialized capabilities.

Today's leading systems optimize for different strengths—including technical accuracy, emotional understanding, conversational intelligence, expressiveness, and robustness. One model that excels at repeating booking reference numbers, bank account details, or complex pharmaceutical names may struggle to produce emotionally expressive speech. Another may sound remarkably natural but be less reliable on precision-oriented tasks.

Sources indicate that as voice AI matures, measuring progress increasingly requires evaluating these capabilities independently rather than collapsing them into a single overall score. In our TTS evaluations, no system configuration ranked among the top five across all eight capability groups—underscoring why there is no single "best" voice model.

Sources indicate that speech-to-Speech models showed the widest variation of any category we evaluated. Some systems recognized emotion exceptionally well but struggled to respond naturally. We found that access to audio did not guarantee that agents used the paralinguistic information it contained. Some systems remained largely transcript-driven, relying on the words being spoken while overlooking cues such as tone, pacing, hesitation, emphasis, and volume.

In a recent development, humans naturally use these cues to infer confidence, uncertainty, frustration, sarcasm, and empathy. Today's models often miss them.

Industry observers note that imagine a banking agent asking whether you recognize a potentially fraudulent transaction. A confident "Yes" and a hesitant "…yes…" may have completely different meanings, even though the transcript is identical. Humans recognize that difference immediately. Many of today's voice models do not.

Recent findings suggest that many established benchmarks are nearing their limits and don't reflect real-world conditions. Models still struggle with accented speech, overlapping speakers, emotion, background noise, and longer conversations. In our evaluation, performance varies far more across leading open-source and proprietary models than traditional benchmarks suggest. In one example, transcription word error rates on noise-backed speech were roughly four times higher than on music-backed speech, showing how a single background-audio score can hide the real failure mode.

In preliminary research, we found signs that some models may be optimized for established public benchmarks. Several reproduced known errors in reference transcripts, followed arbitrary spelling conventions, and even reconstructed masked words that were not present in the audio.

Industry observers note that LLMs are now widely used to evaluate text-based models, but our findings suggest that speech-language models (SLMs) should be used more carefully for voice evaluation. When we compared leading SLMs with trained human raters on text-to-speech assessments, agreement was highest on tasks with clear, verifiable answers, such as pronunciation accuracy.

Recent findings suggest that agreement declined on more subjective evaluations. SLMs sometimes appeared to infer emotion from text-based contextual cues, and agreement was weakest for open-ended judgments such as whether a voice fit an acting role or maintained a consistent identity. Automated evaluators can be valuable for well-defined tasks, but they are not yet a substitute for human listeners when judgments depend on acoustic-context, perception, and social interpretation.

As voice becomes one of AI's defining interfaces, speed and technical accuracy alone will no longer determine which systems succeed. The models people ultimately choose will be those that can understand, express, and respond like humans—not just under ideal benchmark conditions, but across the complexity of real-world conversation.

According to recent reports, for decades, speech AI has advanced by optimizing against quantitative metrics on standardized benchmarks; from WER for transcription accuracy to objective perceptual metrics like PESQ and DNSMOS for speech quality. We hope Real World VoiceEQ can extend this paradigm by providing a human-grounded metric for evaluating the components of synthetic voice interactions.

Read the full technical report and explore the public leaderboards—or get in touch to learn how Hume can evaluate your voice model or agent using Real World VoiceEQ, or design custom evaluations tailored to your specific use case.

Breaking: The Ecosystem is the Answer: Docker, the Blueprint Alliance, and the Importance of Collaboration in the Agentic Era

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, the average global Fortune 500 enterprise had fewer than 15 AI agents in use.
  • Today, most security leaders face an agentic Sophie’s choice: allow AI adoption without the right controls and hope for the best, or block it and become the obstacle to a priority the business has already set (while adoption continues in the shadows, anyway).
  • It has been revealed that but there is a third option, one in which organizations fully tap into the transformative power of agentic agents without having to live in fear of a catastrophic security failure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, the average global Fortune 500 enterprise had fewer than 15 AI agents in use. Gartner expects that number to explode to more than 150,000 by 2028. Only 13 percent of organizations think they have the right governance for today, and AI is evolving and moving faster than any other technology paradigm in our history.

Today, most security leaders face an agentic Sophie’s choice: allow AI adoption without the right controls and hope for the best, or block it and become the obstacle to a priority the business has already set (while adoption continues in the shadows, anyway).

It has been revealed that but there is a third option, one in which organizations fully tap into the transformative power of agentic agents without having to live in fear of a catastrophic security failure. The good news is history has already shown how to get there.

Historically, technology adoption has followed a reliable pattern. A capability spreads, each vendor and team builds its own approach, the inconsistency becomes expensive and ineffective, leading the industry to agree to a shared baseline. Adoption then accelerates.

Take the credit card industry, for example. The massive credit brands each ran their own security programs, and merchants had to satisfy every one. This was, of course, cumbersome for the vendors, but also for the customers, too. Every time a customer wanted to adopt a new technology, they had to manually build out security and adoption aims, adding significant adoption and procurement delays.

According to recent reports, rather than continue on their own, the credit card companies came together to create PCI DSS 1.0 in December 2004 and formed the PCI Security Standards Council in 2006. Buyers now had one thing to ask for, and auditors had one thing to check. Collaboration overcame complexity, and everyone benefited.

Security-minded technologists can find another example closer to home in the Center for Internet Security (CIS). In the early days of the internet, cybersecurity was a veritable wild west. Enter the CIS, which was founded in 2000 because the industry lacked prescriptive, recognized hardening standards. To this day, each CIS Benchmark is built by consensus among volunteer experts, vendors, and academics.

According to recent reports, docker itself is no stranger to the development and furthering of shared standards. As just one example, in 2015, Docker contributed its image format and runC runtime to the Open Container Initiative. A shared baseline at the runtime layer let registries, runtimes, and clouds interoperate.

Each of these examples played a different role: PCI mandated, CIS guided, and OCI standardized.

Agents will need elements of all three.

It has been revealed that agents are in the everyone-builds-their-own phase. Each product solves a real piece of the problem, but which piece, and how the pieces fit, is rarely clear. “Agent governance” or even “AI governance” can mean almost anything.

Adoption is incremental. A developer allows common commands, widens filesystem access, then connects GitHub, a cloud tool and an MCP server, each through a prompt that makes sense on its own. The logs mostly record that the developer acted. Security is often the last to know.

In a recent development, much of the risk is familiar. Shadow adoption looks a lot like early SaaS and cloud. Credential sprawl and supply chain exposure are old problems. Inventory, least privilege, audit, and joiner-mover-leaver discipline still apply.

Several things are upcoming, however:.

Existing controls still matter, but they were not built for this mix of programmability, access, and autonomy.

As with the credit industry and PCI, cybersecurity and the CIS, and containerization and OCI, collaboration offers the answer to this upcoming era of complexity. That’s why Docker is not just focused on building tools like Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance, but in taking an ecosystem-centric approach to problem solving for our customers. Docker is already a founding participant in multiple initiatives aimed at developing valuable reference architectures for AI security workflows, including the Blueprint Alliance and Agent Baseline.

Both start from the same premise: no single vendor or enforcement point can solve this.

The Blueprint Alliance sets out how the pieces fit together. Okta, AWS, CrowdStrike, Databricks, Docker, Google Cloud, Lovable, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Wiz and Zscaler are founding members, with GE Appliances and World Central Kitchen as strategic advisors. The open, multi-vendor reference architecture answers four questions: Where are my agents? What can they do? What are they doing? How do I respond? Members have committed to interoperability testing over MCP, OCSF, SSF and CAEP, and to publishing reference integrations.

Sources indicate that agent Baseline sets out what each piece must do and how to verify it. It fills the gap between threat lists, which say what can go wrong, and the capabilities an enterprise needs in place. It defines six outcomes (Discover, Constrain, Authorize, Observe, Validate and Respond) and 35 open, versioned controls, each with a permanent identifier you can cite in an audit finding or RFP response. Docker, Snyk and Keycard drafted it, and the current release is v1.0-draft. Controls stay where they already live, in the identity provider, the sandbox and the SIEM.

Blueprint says how the pieces connect. Agent Baseline says what must be true and can be checked. Both advise starting with discovery before policy, and testing the kill switch before you need it.

For partners, the roles are defined. The Alliance whitepaper assigns integrators the operating model: assessing a customer’s current stack against the architecture, assigning ownership across the pillars, tiering risk, and running lifecycle and compliance over time. Technology partners get a published target to integrate against, and the reference integrations cross vendor lines by design. The partners who can design, integrate and operate across those lines are the ones customers keep.

Most Alliance members govern agents from the outside: who the agent is, what it can reach, and what it is observed doing. Docker governs the inside: the environment where the agent executes. As agents move from suggesting actions to taking them, trust has to extend beyond the model to the places where they run. Docker has helped define a shared baseline for the runtime before, and now we’re working with the Alliance and our partners to make that baseline concrete, open, and testable in the age of agents.

The execution environment is where policy gets enforced and evidence gets produced.

That boundary is where policy gets enforced and evidence gets produced. The Alliance whitepaper notes that without runtime support to pause an agent without collateral impact, API-driven containment “provides a false sense of security.” Agent Baseline’s CON-03 calls for isolated, confined execution, which is the job of Docker Sandboxes, while Docker MCP Gateway and Docker Hardened Images cover tool access and the supply chain.The Secure Software Factory reference architecture, drafted in part by Docker authors, applies Agent Baseline to agents that ship code.

Baselines let adoption move faster, not slower. Security and platform leaders can assess against the baseline today. Agent Baseline controls are citable, and Okta offers an AI Blueprint Assessment Tool. Partners can start with the Docker Navigator Partner Program, which rewards AI governance work, and with the reference integrations the Alliance publishes. Docker’s VP of Partners Leon Jones explains the program here. Download the blueprint at blueprintalliance.ai and read the controls at agentbaseline.org.

Docker’s WeAreDevelopers keynote indicates how Sandboxes, Kits, and Cloud Sandboxes give AI agents strong isolation and reproducible authority.

According to recent reports, give AI coding agents live web access with the Firecrawl kit for Docker Sandboxes. Learn to search, scrape, and crawl websites with network controls.

In a recent development, A container shares the host kernel. Docker Sandboxes are microVMs with their own kernel and private Docker Engine. See how they differ and when to use each.

Docker partners with ActiveState to continue to provide one standard for trusted content across everything you and your teams build on.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Devuan-based distro swaps Wayland for XLibre and i3, with Xfce waiting if the tiling gets tiresome.
  • Omaxian OS is only at version 0.1, but it already takes a distinctly unconventional route through the Linux desktop.
  • The brand-new Linux desktop distro describes itself as "the Omarchy desktop on X11 — as a shell for your Debian, or as a whole OS." That's not quite the impression that we came away with, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Devuan-based distro swaps Wayland for XLibre and i3, with Xfce waiting if the tiling gets tiresome.

Omaxian OS is only at version 0.1, but it already takes a distinctly unconventional route through the Linux desktop.

The brand-new Linux desktop distro describes itself as "the Omarchy desktop on X11 — as a shell for your Debian, or as a whole OS." That's not quite the impression that we came away with, though.

Like most distros, Omaxian is available as an ISO file you can install and use. Alternatively, Omaxian Shell can be installed on an existing Debian-family distro without replacing the underlying operating system.

The OS release is codenamed "Trans-Siberian Shaman," and the GitHub project repository indicates work going back just a few weeks. No LLM coding assistant is credited on the project page, but we looked inside some of the test scripts, and as well as being verbose and hard to read, they also credit "Grok Bot." Omarchy itself is of course built with LLM assistance, and as we reported last month, so is the new Daemonarchy FreeBSD-based desktop project.

Omaxian is styled after Omarchy, and it includes some of the same tools – and optional support for LLMs – but it's not based on the same tech. Instead of Arch, it's based on Devuan 6, the current version of the systemd-free fork of Debian. Omaxian eschews Hyprland, and indeed Wayland altogether: it opts for an X11 tiling window manager – in this case, i3. i3  first appeared in 2009, so it's been around much longer than Hyprland. Omaxian's configuration also understands familiar keystrokes such as Alt+F4 to close a window. For us, that's a significant usability win.

It has been revealed that the window manager isn't running on top of X.org. Omaxian uses the 2025 fork, the fresh XLibre X11 server. This is a controversial project led by a controversial developer, which will be enough for some people to want to avoid Omaxian as a whole. The latest release of GhostBSD uses XLibre too, though.

Sources indicate that way back in 2021, The Register reported on Omarchy creator David Heinemeier Hansson's firm banning political discussions, and things have only got more vexed since. Just as DHH has attracted some notoriety for his now right-wing views, his Linux is similarly opinionated. If the associations surrounding Omarchy and XLibre put you off, Omaxian's combination of the two probably won't win you over.

The flipside is that if you don't care about the political views, but are interested in the idea of a tiling environment set up for power users who embrace LLM coding assistance, then you might like Omaxian. The full distro trades Arch, Wayland, and systemd for a Devuan base, X11, and sysvinit, with APT handling conventional packages. Flatpaks and AppImages are available too.

We tried Omaxian in VirtualBox, but we experienced frequent display corruption. We must give it this: the interface is slightly easier to navigate than Hyprland. One touch that we did like is that if you get tired of the tiling stuff and want to switch back to something more conventional, then Xfce is also installed in the background. Xfce provides Omaxian with a file manager and other accessories, but you can just choose Xfce from the login screen and find yourself back in a simple, familiar, classic desktop environment.

Sources indicate that omaxian is not the sort of environment we're looking for. This vulture isn't a developer and doesn't use LLMs for anything at all. However, lots of people are looking for something like that, as demonstrated by Omarchy's sponsorship. But it's bold, colorful, and significantly different from the mainstream, and that is the sort of thing we do like to see. ®.

Breaking: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I help lead Google's agent skills program, presently with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like go-skills.
  • In Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out.
  • In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why go test -fuzz missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I help lead Google's agent skills program, presently with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like go-skills. To keep that many skill files consistent, I wrote skill-lint, a standalone Go CLI that checks SKILL.md files and applies LLM-generated line edits before they ship. Even with skill-lint's own unit and fuzz test suite, a small slice or line-number mistake inside its Markdown parsers or edit applier can sit dormant until an unusual file or edit range triggers a runtime panic in the linter.

In Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out. To hunt for crashes, I compiled key functions from my code to see which panic traps survived optimization, and Gemini 4 Argon translated the path to each trap into rules for the Z3 constraint solver. An LLM-written solver model isn't a sound proof system, but it gives the agent an independent way to reason about control flow and synthesize concrete Go reproducers, and every crash it finds is real because go test runs the offending bytes directly. That workflow caught all three bugs I planted in test parsers and turned up three latent bugs in skill-lint.

In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why go test -fuzz missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow.

A recent post from Anthropic showed how formal verification catches latent bugs in C and C++ by having frontier AI models write machine-checked Rocq proofs across OSS-Fuzz libraries. Instead of sampling random inputs like a fuzzer, a formal tool works backward from each failure condition to solve for the exact input that triggers it. Full theorem proving is still too heavy for most day-to-day Go projects, so I wanted to see how much of that bug-hunting power an agent can get from an LLM and a constraint solver in about a minute per function.

In a recent development, in C and C++, reading or writing past the end of a buffer corrupts memory. Go catches out-of-bounds access at runtime instead, compiling every slice or index operation it can't prove safe into an explicit branch to runtime.panicBounds that panics, crashing the process unless recovered.

Before generating machine code, Go's SSA prove pass already eliminates most of those checks by tracking slice lengths and loop variables. That optimization pass leaves behind only the runtime.panicBounds traps the compiler couldn't rule out on its own, giving the solver a short list of candidate crash sites to target.

I compiled each target with GOOS=linux GOARCH=riscv64 go build -gcflags="-S -d=ssa/check_bce/debug=1" (-S prints the assembly listing and ssa/check_bce/debug=1 logs every surviving bounds check) and passed both the Go source and the disassembly to the model. Looking at Go source alone, you can't see which bounds checks the compiler already removed or where a register gets truncated to 8 bits; in the disassembly, both show up. I targeted RISC-V because it's the instruction set Anthropic's post targets for its Rocq proofs, and Go cross-compiles to it out of the box.

Industry observers note that from there, Argon read the Go source and disassembly and returned a Z3 script modeling the path to each surviving trap, along with a patched function whenever it flagged a bug. Z3 then checked whether those constraints could be satisfied, and whenever it found a crashing input, go test replayed those bytes against the real function. Using an LLM saved me from translating assembly into solver constraints by hand. Argon's translation dominated the runtime, at about a minute per function, while Z3 itself finished in milliseconds.

Welcome Inkling by Thinking Machines

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that update: Inkling 2 Small is here!
  • Inkling is Thinking Machines' family of open multimodal models, and it now spans two generations on the Hub:.
  • In this post, we start with the first-generation architecture, then walk through what changed in Inkling 2 Small and how to run it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that update: Inkling 2 Small is here! 🤗 Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, the next generation of the Inkling family. We have updated this post with a newly introduced section on Inkling 2 Small, covering what changed in the architecture and how to run it with transformers.

Inkling is Thinking Machines' family of open multimodal models, and it now spans two generations on the Hub:.

In this post, we start with the first-generation architecture, then walk through what changed in Inkling 2 Small and how to run it. The rest of the post covers inference, use cases, post-training, and deployment, with examples built on the first-generation checkpoints.

Inkling is the first large open model with ~1T parameters and 1M context window to natively receive image, text, and audio inputs, trained on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio and video. It’s focused on reasoning across modalities such as audio, images, and text. It is intended for domain adaptation via fine-tuning. We’ve tinkered (pun intended) with this model to build some demos and explore the architecture, and we think it’s great for building a new wave of multimodal reasoning apps.

Inkling is a decoder-only multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) model with 975B total and 41B active parameters. There are a lot of things going on, so let’s break each part down:.

Here’s a quick glance of the architecture.

Relative attention: Instead of RoPE, which is the usual method to inject positional information in transformers models, Inkling uses relative attention to encode position information. Each attention layer learns position directly in the attention logits. Aside from key-query-values, there's a fourth projection producing a per-token, per-head relative feature R. This projection tensor is then tweaked with distance information (distance between the key and the query vector) and propagated into the attention module.

Hybrid attention: The decoder layers alternate between global attention (attending to the full context length at once) and sliding window attention (attending to a fixed context window in a sliding fashion). The architecture has a pattern of 5:1 sliding window to global attention layers. This hybrid attention scheme provides efficiency in computation. The final layer uses global attention to help build feature-rich representations.

Short convolution: The model uses a distinctive short 1D convolution, or SConv over the hidden states. SConv reads the current token and the previous W-1 hidden states, with W being the sliding window size. The intuition here is that SConv helps with local attention while freeing the attention and MoE modules from local representations.

Recent findings suggest that moE with shared experts sink: In Inkling, the router scores both routed experts and shared experts. Top-k selection is performed over 6 experts, plus 2 shared experts always active.

Vision understanding: The model includes a simple hierarchical MLP patchifier consisting of several linear layers. Each layer merges pixels progressively, until the final layer produces one embedding per patch.

Audio understanding: The architecture employs a discretized mel spectrogram, where each of the audio chunks (of 100 ms) are converted to the mel scale and then classified into the exact mel spectrogram bin.

The multimodal towers are relatively simple modules, unlike other models that employ separate encoders for each modality. Each image patch passes through the image embedding tower and the audio chunk is passed through the audio embedding tower to get both media embeddings. Image inputs also include an additional temporal dimension for video processing. We expect this capability to be useful for downstream fine-tuning, but we haven’t evaluated out-of-the-box video performance. The tower folds the patch grid, a small local block of neighboring tokens is stacked into the channel dimension and goes through hMLP. The audio waveform is converted to mel scale, which is then classified into a discrete mel bin. These mel bin values are embedded in the audio embedding tower and the embeddings are then summed to construct the final audio input.

Inkling 2 is the next generation of the family. It takes text and image inputs (but no audio), and generates text. It keeps the core ideas of Inkling's decoder:.

Almost everything around that core was redesigned, though. The layers read from the residual stream differently, attention is bounded and gated, the MoE is simpler and wider, and the vision tower is now a real vision transformer.

Here's how the two generations compare:.

Let's go over the most notable changes together:.

According to recent reports, block attention residuals: In a standard transformer, every layer adds its output to the residual stream, and the next layer reads it. Inkling 2 has no single residual stream. Instead, it groups its 48 layers into 8 blocks of 6 and keeps one sum per block:.

It has been revealed that A sublayer (attention or MLP) doesn't read one of these sums directly. It attends over depth, which means at each token position, it treats the finished block summaries plus the current partial block as a short sequence, and takes a softmax-weighted mix of them.

The query is a single learned vector per sublayer. The keys and values are the RMS-normalized block summaries at that position. So the weights differ from token to token, depending on what each block wrote there.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, each sublayer learns how much to draw from each earlier stage of the network, rather than always reading the sum of everything. By the last layer, there are up to 9 sources to choose from (the embeddings, 7 finished blocks and the current partial block), and the final norm reads its input the same way. Global attention layers learn three queries, so their query, key and value projections can each draw on a different mix of blocks.

Dynamic short convolutions: The short convolutions on keys and values in the global attention layers are now dynamic. The 4 taps of each convolution are a fixed learned weight plus a per-token weight predicted from the input, shared within each key/value head. So the model can change, token by token, how much local context goes into each key and value. All short convolutions also rescale their residual sum to keep its variance stable through depth.

A leaner, wider MoE: Each layer has 384 routed experts with 8 active per token, and the shared experts are gone.

A upcoming vision encoder: Inkling encoded images with a lightweight hierarchical MLP. Inkling 2 uses a 23-layer vision transformer based on the Perception Encoder. It has the following properties:.

Several images are packed into one sequence, and each image only attends to itself.

Inkling 2 uses the same Auto classes as Inkling. Make sure to have updated transformers to run the model.

Inkling comes with day-0 transformers support and is supported in major inference engines like SGLang and vLLM.

In a recent development, this model is huge. The bf16 checkpoint requires 2 TB of VRAM, while the nvfp4 version requires 600 GB of VRAM. You can try the model through serverless inference routers like Inference Providers, or use ggml quants for local deployment with llama.cpp.

Industry observers note that the easiest way to infer with transformers directly is to use the any-to-any pipeline. You can use either the 16 bit "thinkingmachines/Inkling" on Hopper or later GPUs, or the quantized NVFP4 checkpoint "thinkingmachines/Inkling-NVFP4" on Blackwell Nvidia GPUs. Make sure to have the latest version of transformers (5.14.0 was released today) (pip install -U transformers).

After initializing the pipeline, you can pass in the prompt as follows.

Going one level lower, you can use Auto classes. For inference, you can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class for models and AutoProcessor class for processors. For different reasoning tasks, the tokenizer takes in a reasoning_effort argument. Existing options for reasoning effort are "none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", and "max".

For multimodal inference, you can use the same classes. We provide example snippets for each different modality in the model card.

Inkling also takes in audio input. Below is an example inference snippet, which still uses the same AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

For more realistic parallel deployment in a cluster of several nodes, please refer to the Slurm section below.

SGLang is one of the fastest deployment frameworks for Inkling at the time of release, as it includes a custom model implementation. The launch command below shards the model across 8 GPUs and serves an OpenAI-compatible API on port 30000.

Match --tp-size to your GPU count. Add --mem-fraction-static (e.g. 0.85) if you need to leave more headroom for the KV cache.

vLLM is strong for production serving. A single vllm serve command downloads the weights from the Hub, shards the model across your GPUs with tensor parallelism, and starts an OpenAI-compatible server on port 8000. You can view the vLLM Recipe for the model here to customize to your hardware.

In practice, you might need multiple nodes and a distribution tool like SLURM (see below). Key parameters are --tensor-parallel-size to the number of GPUs on your node, and use --max-model-len to cap the context window if you hit KV-cache memory limits.

It has been revealed that you can infer with this model using several inference providers through Hugging Face. You can see all the code snippets to consume here. Below you can see how to use with the OpenAI client.

In a recent development, using the “:auto” suffix routes to your preferred provider in your settings; you can also use “cheapest” or “:fastest” as well. For this release, we cover the inference costs for 2 hours within the release for everyone.

Note: audio support in Inference Providers is work in progress and will be added shortly.

In a recent development, you can use llama.cpp to run quantized versions of the model on limited hardware. Unsloth have quantized the model down to 1-bit precision, reducing VRAM consumption by 95% over the original model.

Sources indicate that this starts an OpenAI-compatible server running at http://localhost:8080/v1 that you connect to in your preferred tool or clients. Heading there, you can start chatting with the model, and set it up with your favorite MCPs, pass in images or files conveniently and more!

Industry observers note that llama cpp also ships with a built-in UI that supports tools, mcp, and agentic workloads. Checkout Inkling running at 1-bit precision in the llama app:.

Inkling GGUFs are also runnable in Unsloth Studio with dynamic 1-bit GGUFs which retain ~74.2% of top-1% accuracy whilst being 86% smaller.

In a recent development, pi is a minimal coding agent harness you can use with different language models. You can use Pi with either an inference engine server endpoint, such as llama.cpp, or with Inference Providers on Hugging Face by adding this to your ~/.pi/agent/models.json after installation.

Then you can start Pi in your project directory by calling pi and you’re good to go! In this demo, we give the model a hard math reasoning problem and it uses tools in pi to solve it.

Inkling is focused on broad multimodality reasoning and low token consumption, so try it out with document processing or audio tasks.

It has been revealed that MTP adds extra layers to the model that predict several tokens at once, not just the next one. During inference, the extra layers act as “drafters” for speculative decoding, speeding up generation without compromising performance. With MTP, you get the exact same generated outputs, multipliers in generation speed-up at small memory cost in VRAM (due to serving the drafter). Thinking Machines also provides an MTP drafter with this release.

We have prepared a small suite of reasoning questions from expert-level sources and university entrance exams. We have taken photos of the screen with watermarks in the screenshot to challenge the model. The model has solved all of them on high one, failed one in highest and medium reasoning efforts, so we provide a link to the model answers for you to check out how the model sounds and provide the number of tokens the model has taken to solve each of them. Note that we provide no system prompts in these vibe evals, and these reasoning questions should often be run with a good system prompt. The vibe eval images and results live here.

Sources indicate that we have vibe-evaluated the model on some audio reasoning examples from BigBenchAudio and a few multilingual audio examples of GlobeAudio (Russian and Chinese multi-choice questions asking the last word in transcription). The BigBenchAudio examples we tested consist of logical statements and questions that either ask for formal fallacies (whether an argument can be logically deduced from the context given in audio) or object counting (stating multiple distinctive objects in the audio, asking for the total count of a certain one). Although this benchmark is initially made for speech-to-speech reasoning, we just want to see audio reasoning capabilities of this model. For GlobeAudio, the questions are relatively straightforward, so we ran with reasoning efforts of 0.1. We ran the first example of each language within GlobeAudio. All tests pass on all questions and efforts, except for second formal fallacy example on lowest effort, so we only provide the number of tokens spent in each question against reasoning effort. Vibe eval results and audio files live here.

In a recent development, if you would like to use Inkling for post-training, Thinking Machines have built tinker, a managed tool for post-training open weight models. Their cookbook includes examples for fine-tuning, distillation, and reinforcement learning.

We post trained Inkling with tinker and OpenEnv, an agentic RL environment tool. We used the ECHO algorithm that trains a model to predict the environment without a verifier, applying next-token cross-entropy loss to tokens produced by the environment, alongside the usual policy learning on agent actions. This teaches the policy an implicit world model without requiring a separate model, teacher, or additional rollouts. Check out the example.

If you’re working with Transformers Reinforcement Learning we suggest using Inkling as a teacher model in a knowledge distillation setup. For example, take advantage of Inkling’s document understanding abilities to improve the performance of a smaller (on-device) model. In this example, we use the transformer reinforcement learning library and the GOLD algorithm to distill knowledge. GOLD is handy here because it matches token logits between different tokenizers, so you can distill to any model on the hub.

Below you can find each Inkling checkpoint as well as their VRAM requirements.

To deploy Inkling on a cluster, we provide SLURM scripts serving with transformers API, as well as how to query the endpoint with different modalities. You can adapt these scripts to vLLM or SGlang by updating the commands. These scripts live here.

You can deploy an Inkling-Small NVFP4 checkpoint using Inference Endpoints. We provide a pre-tested configuration to deploy it on 8 RTX PRO 6000s with an aggregated VRAM of·768 GB, giving large space for KV cache, costs $ 22 per hourly uptime (scales to zero when unused). To deploy, run hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4 using the Hugging Face CLI or alternatively, head to https://endpoints.huggingface.co/new/thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4. With this setup, you can get 140 TPS (single user inference, prepared for multi-user support with continuous batching).

Once the endpoint is up, you can query as follows.

Releasing a natively multimodal model (text, vision, and audio) open-weights is a huge step forward for the open-source AI ecosystem! Having variable and controllable thinking effort built into a MoE architecture makes Inkling a really attractive foundation for fine-tuning. Excited to test out the smaller 12B active parameter variant for local agent workflows at https://geometrydashsubzero.io.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that score, a CNCF Sandbox project, recently joined the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program to strengthen the security of its container images and release pipeline.
  • In September 2025, the CNCF confirmed a partnership with Docker to expand infrastructure support for project maintainers through the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program.
  • This aligned closely with the discussions held at the Maintainer Summit NA 2025 in Atlanta, which centered on increasing collaboration across CNCF projects and demonstrating security best practices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that score, a CNCF Sandbox project, recently joined the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program to strengthen the security of its container images and release pipeline. In this post, the Score maintainers share what we adopted (Docker Hub, Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, the Docker GitHub Builder, and OIDC connections), the results we measured, and how other open source projects, within the CNCF and beyond, can apply the same practices by default.

In September 2025, the CNCF confirmed a partnership with Docker to expand infrastructure support for project maintainers through the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The partnership gives CNCF projects access to Docker’s security scanning tools, container registry, and best-practice resources at no cost.

This aligned closely with the discussions held at the Maintainer Summit NA 2025 in Atlanta, which centered on increasing collaboration across CNCF projects and demonstrating security best practices.

The Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program supports non-commercial open source projects with Docker tooling and infrastructure.

Before: Score publishes different container images: the CLIs of score-compose, score-k8s, score-helm and score-radius; and the sample-score-app used for demos and testing. We previously published them in the GitHub Container Registry here.

After: Through the DSOS Program, we now publish these images on Docker Hub, which increases their visibility and gives the community a verified, trusted source.

All the container images are now available on Docker Hub.

The program also provides usage analytics that show how the community uses these images. Here is an example:.

Before: As a CNCF project, Score follows the OpenSSF best practices. In addition, the OpenSSF Scorecard GitHub Action runs continuously. This was a solid foundation, but we had no dedicated security scanning tool in place.

It has been revealed that after: The DSOS Program gave us access to Docker Scout, which we now use in our pull requests and on our container registry (Docker Hub). This gives us clear visibility into the CVEs introduced or fixed by each pull request and release.

The following GitHub Actions step uses docker/scout-action on every pull request to compare the image built from the PR branch with the one built from the main branch:.

Here is an example of a comment posted by this docker/scout-action step in a recent Pull Request:.

The comment details the comparison between the two images (before versus after): size, packages updated, added or removed, CVEs introduced and resolved, and compliance with our policies in place (run as non-root, no critical CVEs, no packages with AGPL v3 licences).

The analysis goes beyond the images themselves: it also covers the Go libraries and binaries they contain.

The Docker Scout console also provides a single view of CVEs, packages, base images, and policies across all of our container images, which makes it easy to see what is used where, and in which version.

When Docker made Hardened Images freely available under Apache 2.0, we saw an opportunity to simplify our security posture while staying compatible with our existing Dockerfiles and workflows, even though we were already using multi-stage builds and distroless base images.

Recent findings suggest that docker Hardened Images are minimal, security-focused container base images designed to reduce inherited risk in downstream projects. They are built and maintained with security and transparency as defaults, and offer:.

The migration was straightforward.

Industry observers note that take the score-radius CLI, which used a golang:alpine and a distroless images and now uses dhi.io/golang and dhi.io/static images. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal:.

It has been revealed that in the associated PR here, image size dropped by 0.3 MB while the number of packages stayed the same and the CVE count remained at 0. We could have stayed with Debian, but chose to move to an Alpine base image (DHI provides the two options):.

The same applies to the NodeJS sample-score-app, which used nodejs on top of an alpine image and now uses a dhi.io/node image. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal:.

In the associated PR here, 22 packages were removed (including the package manager and the shell), along with 2 CVEs:.

Note: We were able to present a short walkthrough of our DHI integration during the CNCF webinar held on January 23, 2026, which accompanied the Docker Hardened Images announcement for CNCF projects.

Although not directly part of the DSOS Program, we took the opportunity to adopt the latest docker/github-builder GitHub reusable workflow to release our container images.

This model provides a build pipeline maintained in the Docker organization, with a version-controlled BuildKit environment, multi-platform builds distributed across runners where beneficial, and signed SLSA provenance recording both the source commit and the builder identity.

The trade-off is intentional. You retain control over when the build runs and which inputs it uses, while the build implementation itself lives in the Docker-maintained workflow rather than in per-repository job steps.

Before, the GitHub Actions workflow to release our container images was using this sequence of actions:.

After, this same workflow is now only using the reusable workflow docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml:.

In a recent development, docker GitHub Builder gives us a Docker-maintained build pipeline with signed SLSA provenance and SBOM attestations, helping consumers verify the builder identity and trace images back to their source commit. Signing uses GitHub OIDC, so we don’t need to manage long-lived signing keys. With caching enabled in our workflow, cache entries are also signed and verified before reuse, helping protect against cache poisoning. See the Docker GitHub Builder documentation for more information about its security model.

The following command verifies the signature on the attestation manifest for the selected image platform:.

According to recent reports, most recently, with an update released on July 21, 2026, Docker introduced OIDC connections. This feature allows pulls and pushes to Docker Hub to use a short-lived token instead of a long-lived Organization Access Token (OAT).

According to recent reports, an OIDC connection establishes a trust relationship between Docker and a trusted third party, so you no longer need to maintain long-lived credentials. Docker exchanges short-lived tokens with the other vendor, which can grant fine-grained access to your Docker resources.

By replacing a static, long-lived token with a short-lived one and making it issued on a per-workflow basis, we removed a credential that could otherwise be stolen and misused.

Sources indicate that participating in the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program has been rewarding, and it has helped Score adopt a security-by-default foundation. Using Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, OIDC connections, and the Docker GitHub Builder has strengthened the security posture of our container images and brought broader benefits to the Score projects and repositories.

Industry observers note that if you maintain a CNCF project or any open source project, we encourage you to explore the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The security improvements were measurable, and the onboarding process was straightforward.

The full implementation across the Score repositories is tracked in GitHub concern #376.

Recent findings suggest that attending KubeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City? Feel free to connect with the Score maintainers during the Maintainer Summit on Sunday, Nov 8th and at the Kiosk #P-17B on Thursday, Nov 12th between 10:15am and 2pm, you will see Score in actions with the latest Score Labspace! You can also meet the Docker team at booth #141 in Hall C!

According to recent reports, note: This work was completed after I joined Docker. It was, however, an initiative we wanted to pursue as CNCF project maintainers from the moment it was announced in September 2025, both to improve our security posture and to share what we learned with the broader community.

We hope this post helps you strengthen the security of your own projects.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 173,000 signatures, a few famous billionaires, and absolutely no guarantee they're genuine.

Elon Musk and a bunch of Silicon Valley heavyweights want Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, and they've decided an online petition is the way to make it happen.

An open letter addressed to Nvidia's board had attracted more than 173,000 signatures at the time of writing, just four days after Huang's departure following revelations about his personal relationships, including an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.

The campaign, launched under the banner "Stand with Jensen," calls on Nvidia to reinstate its co-founder and former CEO while an independent investigation establishes the facts, give him a chance to respond to the allegations, and publicly explain why he was forced out.

In a recent development, "For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," the letter reads. "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes.

"Many of us joined because of him. Many of us stayed because of how he treated the work: as something worth getting right, together, at whatever hour it took. This firm is the work of his life. That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now.".

Among the supporters are Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator boss Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. More than 8,000 signatories also identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to roughly a fifth of its workforce.

Sources indicate that however, how many of those signatures are genuine is anyone's guess. The site doesn't verify names or employers, so there's nothing stopping someone from signing as Musk, Huang, or Nvidia's entire board if they fancy it.

The campaign follows Huang's resignation on November 12, ending his 33-year reign at the GPU giant he co-founded in 1993. His departure came after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who US intelligence suspects of spying for Beijing, and a separate alleged relationship with an Nvidia employee.

Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has been handed the unenviable job of running the tech giant while its board searches for a permanent replacement. Huang's departure has left the chipmaker facing something of an identity crisis, with rivals undoubtedly watching the chaos with interest.

It has been revealed that huang himself may not be ready to hang up his leather jacket. According to the Financial Times, the former CEO has discussed a possible comeback with associates, while an ally is reportedly assembling a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.

The effort could even involve seeking support from the White House, although Washington appears rather less enthusiastic about the prospect.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shake-up" and should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also wants answers about whether Nvidia knowingly allowed advanced AI chips to reach China in breach of US export restrictions.

In a recent development, none of that seems to have put off Huang's supporters. "He has erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company," Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick said.

Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, giving investors their first major opportunity to grill management about the leadership crisis.

It has been revealed that whether the board will be swayed by a petition full of unverified names is another matter. Running one of the world's most valuable companies is, after all, not supposed to be a popularity contest. ®.

Docker and ActiveState Extending Secure Defaults to the Packages Developers Install

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Trusted content is the foundation security-conscious organizations expect all builds to start from.
  • Teams building on a secure foundation now want the same assurance for the open source their applications install.
  • Docker is committed to one standard for trusted content across everything teams build on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trusted content is the foundation security-conscious organizations expect all builds to start from. Docker has made that possible for everyone by providing the foundation free. Docker Hardened Images (DHI) are open source under Apache 2.0, with a catalog of 4,000+ minimal images (and growing) built from source and continuously maintained by Docker. The catalog also carries customizable Helm charts and over 65,000 hardened system packages. For most services, adopting DHI is as simple as changing the FROM line.

Teams building on a secure foundation now want the same assurance for the open source their applications install. That open source is a different layer of the supply chain, where thousands of upstream projects are pulled in at build time by pip, npm and Maven, and by coding agents as well.

Docker is committed to one standard for trusted content across everything teams build on. A latest partnership with ActiveState, the organization that has been securing open source since 1997, extends that standard to the packages themselves. Together, we give teams the same assurance on both layers, from the hardened images Docker maintains to the packages developers and their agents install on them. Once configured, the integration allows developers and AI coding assistants to continue using familiar package managers and development workflows, while approved dependencies are sourced through governed repositories rather than directly from public registries.

Most applications still start from a large, generic base image, and the cost of that choice keeps growing. A large image increases the attack surface and accumulates stale dependencies, and the CVEs it generates land on developers long after the image was chosen. By removing unnecessary packages, rebuilding components from source and continuously maintaining the image, Docker Hardened Images reduce the vulnerabilities inherited from the container foundation. Images can achieve near-zero known CVEs, which means less remediation work and less scanner noise before application code is introduced. The hardening and patching are handled once in the foundation, for every service that builds on it.

According to recent reports, above the base image sit the dependencies an application brings with it. DHI secures the operating system packages and the language runtime that ship in the image. The application’s own libraries are pulled in at build time by its package managers from public registries, where trust is assumed and seldom verified. That layer needs what the image now has, a source that admits only the versions a team has approved and stands behind the fix when one of them needs it. Coding agents now pull those packages too. As Mark Lechner, CISO wrote in April, a compromised dependency pulled by an agent has the same blast radius as a compromised developer machine.

Industry observers note that this year’s supply chain incidents have followed one pattern. As Lechner documented, attackers steal developer credentials, use them to poison trusted packages, and the compromised packages steal more credentials. The axios compromise earlier this year put two backdoored versions of a library downloaded 83 million times a week into circulation for about three hours. Most of these attacks burn out within hours. A build that resolves fresh from a public registry, with no lockfile or cooldown in front of it, has nothing between it and a version published an hour ago. The slower failure is the vulnerability that surfaces in one of those libraries months later, when no one outside the team is accountable for the fix. Either way, without trusted content on both layers, the risk lands on your team.

Docker Hardened Images are the foundation, and Docker stands behind them. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, with full, unsuppressed CVE visibility. A security team can see what is in the image and how it was built. For teams that need remediation on a predictable clock, DHI adds a 7-day SLA on critical and high CVEs, FIPS and STIG variants, and secure customization on its paid tiers.

While DHI secures the image, ActiveState hardens the open source built on it. ActiveState provides the Curated Catalog, a private, policy-governed repository of open source components that security teams curate and developers and AI coding assistants consume safely. The catalog holds only the packages a team has approved. ActiveState compiles every component from original source code in a SLSA Level 3 environment with full provenance and complete SBOMs, in place of pre-compiled binaries from a public registry. When a fix becomes available upstream, ActiveState rebuilds the component and publishes it to the catalog automatically under SLAs of 5 business days for critical CVEs and 10 for highs.

With DHI and the Curated Catalog together, both layers carry provenance, SBOMs and a remediation SLA from the hardened image to the packages built on it. That gives security teams a consistent evidence trail across the software supply chain. The artifact repository teams already run, Artifactory or Nexus, points at the Curated Catalog as its upstream the way it points at PyPI today. Developers keep the same pip and npm workflow, and coding agents are served the governed version. None of this replaces the pinned digests, cooldown periods and sandboxed agents Lechner recommends. It gives those controls a governed source to point at.

AI coding agents are changing how swiftly organizations create software. They can generate applications, select dependencies and initiate builds at a pace that traditional security review processes were never designed to support. Still, faster development should not mean blindly accepting more supply chain risk. Docker Hardened Images reduce the security burden of maintaining container foundations. ActiveState’s Curated Catalog extends governance and managed vulnerability remediation to the open source libraries those applications depend on. The result is a more consistent approach to software supply chain security, with trusted foundations, governed dependencies, verifiable build evidence and clear remediation responsibilities.

The goal is not to add another security checkpoint that causes friction in your build process. It is to make the secure path the easiest path for developers, platform teams and AI coding agents alike.

Security scales when the defaults are strong and the foundation is maintained by a team accountable for it. In an increasingly agent-driven development environment, the security of what gets built depends heavily on the trustworthiness of what those agents are allowed to consume. Docker now resells the ActiveState Curated Catalog alongside DHI, and ActiveState resells DHI to its customers. The hardened image and the packages built on it are both available through Docker.

#23324. Model Routing Is Simple. Until It Isn’t.

📅 15 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1007 w)

Model Routing Is Simple. Until It Isn’t.

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, building a router into your agent sounds like an easy win.
  • According to recent reports, except it’s not.
  • Industry observers note that we expected GPT-4.1 to be cheaper than Claude Sonnet 4.6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, building a router into your agent sounds like an easy win. Send simple requests to cheaper models, reserve expensive ones for harder tasks, or route by specialty — Claude for code, Gemini for multimodal, and so on. A classifier or heuristic makes the call, costs go down, performance stays up. Done.

According to recent reports, except it’s not. Most routing systems assume that model selection is a classification problem. In our experience building routing into agentic systems, what looks like a model-selection problem swiftly becomes a systems optimization problem. Three dimensions made this surprisingly hard for us.

Industry observers note that we expected GPT-4.1 to be cheaper than Claude Sonnet 4.6. It wasn’t.

Sources indicate that across 417 tasks on the AppWorld Test Challenge using the same CodeAct agent, Sonnet cost $79 total ($0.19/task) while GPT-4.1 cost $155 ($0.37/task) — nearly double. On paper, this makes no sense. GPT-4.1’s token pricing is lower on both input and output, and Sonnet takes roughly three times as many reasoning steps to finish the same tasks. By sticker price alone, GPT-4.1 should win easily.

Industry observers note that the explanation? Caching — something most routing discussions ignore entirely. Agent workloads tend to reuse large chunks of context across steps. When cache hit rates are high, effective input costs drop dramatically. Sonnet’s lower cache-read pricing meant it benefited disproportionately from this pattern, enough to overcome both its higher base pricing and its longer trajectories.

The takeaway: actual cost depends on the interaction between the model, the workload, and the serving infrastructure. A router that only looks at pricing sheets is optimizing against the wrong numbers.

Sources indicate that A common routing strategy is to estimate how hard a task is and send harder tasks to stronger models. Intuitive, but it breaks down in two ways.

According to recent reports, first, difficulty is often invisible at routing time. A request like "summarize this contract" looks simple, but might trigger retrieval, compliance checks, tool use, and multiple rounds of refinement before it’s done. Meanwhile, a highly technical prompt might be handled efficiently by a smaller specialized model. You often don’t know how hard a task actually is until execution is underway.

Second, even if you could perfectly estimate difficulty, it’s only one signal among many. In production, routers need to balance cost, latency, model specialization, and reliability simultaneously. Enterprise deployments pile on more: compliance requirements, data residency rules, privacy constraints, approved model lists. A task that would ideally go to one model might need to go elsewhere because of governance — and the router has to handle that gracefully.

Sources indicate that routers aren’t solving one problem. They’re constantly juggling cost, quality, latency, compliance, and reliability all at once.

In a recent development, it’s tempting to think about latency purely in terms of model size — bigger models are slower, smaller ones are faster. But what the user actually experiences depends on much more than that.

According to recent reports, routing itself adds overhead. Infrastructure factors — which hardware a model is running on, whether the cache is warm, how busy the endpoint is — often dominate end-to-end response times. A theoretically faster model can still produce a slower experience if the serving conditions aren’t right.

Then there’s routing granularity. Routing once per task adds minimal overhead. But routing at every step — which gives you more flexibility to adapt mid-execution — means every additional decision point introduces latency and operational complexity.

A router that ignores the serving system is optimizing against the wrong reality.

These lessons shaped how we built our router. The key shift: we stopped treating routing as a classification problem and started treating it as an optimization problem. Rather than asking "which model is best for this task?", our algorithm optimizes across cost, quality, and latency simultaneously — while staying lightweight enough to avoid becoming a bottleneck itself.

The figure below demonstrates the result on the AppWorld Test Challenge with a CodeAct agent. Each blue square is a different configuration of our router, tracing out a cost-accuracy frontier. The notable thing isn't any single point — it's that the router gives you a range of operating points to choose from depending on whether you want to prioritize cost, latency, or accuracy. Configuration 1 (latency-optimized) lands at 84% accuracy for $93 and 83s — a 21% cost reduction and 9% latency reduction compared to running Opus alone, with only a 4% accuracy drop. Configuration 2 pushes cost even lower.

It has been revealed that notice that a standard difficulty-based router (the teal diamond) lands in a similar accuracy range but at higher cost — it doesn't explore the full tradeoff space the way an optimization-based approach can. And because the optimization itself is lightweight (roughly 6 ms and 2 kB of memory per task), the router doesn't become the bottleneck we warned about earlier.

The lesson we took away from this work is that routing isn’t really about choosing models. It’s about optimizing systems. Models are one variable — an important one, but just one among caching behavior, infrastructure state, compliance constraints, and workload patterns.

When routing works well, it’s rarely because it found the "best" model for a given task. It’s because it found the best operating point for the entire system. That’s a harder problem than classification, but it’s the one worth solving.

We’ll be sharing more about the technical details behind our approach in a follow-up post. In the meantime, if you’re building routing into your own agentic systems, we’d love to hear what tradeoffs you’re running into.

This post was influenced by numerous conversations with colleagues, whose thoughtful questions, feedback, and insights helped refine our thinking.

So I've always felt that model routing is a false proposition; it should have been part of the harness all along.

Agreed, routing should disappear into the harness and just be part of the system's execution logic. Our goal is exactly that—making model choice an intrinsic capability rather than a separate concern.
